The bias limitation remains, but v1's explicit concluding caveat that tail improvement need not reduce expected regret outside discrete problems is dropped.

D1.justification: v3 adds code-access links and substantial implementation documentation: MLP layer widths and activations, Adam and stopping details, preprocessing, synthetic-data generation and phase-specific configurations (Section 3 and Appendix D). These are documented access and implementation additions; the linked resources were not inspected. v1's Apple M1 Pro and 16 GB hardware disclosure is removed.

E1.justification: v3 adds synthetic regression and six UCI datasets: Wine Quality, Bike Sharing, Online News, Appliances Energy, Superconductivity and Gas Turbine Emission. It removes v1's LASSO-based model-selection task and replaces the six-asset integer CVaR portfolio problem with continuous, ten-asset mean-variance optimization. Appendix D also adds a network-design scenario with strongly correlated objectives.

E2.justification: The new regression comparisons evaluate unensembled Adam-trained MLPs, least-squares regression and ridge regression against their ensemble variants. v1 Figure 11's comparison of SAA-based ensembles against standalone Wasserstein DRO across ambiguity radii is removed. DRO remains evaluated as a base learner in v3 Figure 16, corresponding to v1 Figure 3.

E3.justification: v3 introduces MLP training/validation splits of 70%/30%, early stopping, standardized real datasets with half-training/half-testing splits, and a million-sample synthetic test set. Its continuous-problem defaults use k1=max(30,n/2), k2=max(30,n/200) and B1=50, whereas v1 used a shared k=max(10,n/200) and B1=20. Most discrete-problem defaults remain unchanged; additional protocols include loss-tail evaluation and larger-subsample network-design controls.

E4.justification: Most original subsample-size, ensemble-size, epsilon, optima-multiplicity and tail-heaviness analyses are retained or relocated. v3 adds comparisons across MLP depths and synthetic input dimensions, plus network-design controls for larger subsamples and strongly correlated objectives (Figures 1, 10–13 and 15). These substantially extend the analysis of capacity sensitivity and conditions limiting ensemble benefits.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over more than 50 repetitions without empirical confidence intervals. v3 adds 95% confidence intervals to regression and stochastic-programming cost plots and specifies 200 independently generated synthetic datasets and 100 real-data permutations. These disclosures do not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments; their former general repetition-count statement is no longer provided.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive regression mean-cost and tail-probability results, together with results for the replacement portfolio task and additional network scenarios. Figure 2 shows markedly lighter ROVE tails on three of six real datasets, while ROVEs underperforms the base learner; Figure 10a also reports a low-capacity ROVEs failure. v1's model-selection, CVaR and standalone-DRO-sweep results are removed. Results under replacement settings do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The majority-vote and two-phase epsilon-optimality architectures remain. Algorithms 1–2 now accept a generic, possibly randomized learner instead of requiring an empirical-objective minimizer. Algorithm 2 permits separate retrieval and voting subsample sizes, k1 and k2, and evaluates candidates using sample-mean loss instead of v1's generic empirical objective. These are adaptations within the retained voting framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten, with changed terminology and mathematical notation throughout. Hyperparameter profiling moves from Section 3.1 to Appendix D.3, regression leads the experimental section, related work gains a main-text section, and Appendix D is reorganized around architectures, problems, profiling and additional results.

P2.justification: v3 introduces numerous regression and tail-probability panels, adds confidence bars, restructures the main optimization figure and redraws retained plots with revised labels and axes. Profiling, light-tail and DRO-base figures move into the appendix, while the standalone-DRO comparison disappears. Typography, title/author layout and figure placement also change substantially.

R1.justification: v3 adds a substantial ensemble-learning discussion covering subagging, boosting and stacking, with citations including Dietterich, Zhou, Wolpert and Chen–Guestrin. It explicitly positions model-level selection against prediction aggregation in existing ensembles. Much of v1's heavy-tail and learning-to-optimize review is retained and moved into Section 4, while Appendix A retains bagging for stochastic optimization.

T1.justification: v3 recasts Theorem 1 using the base learner's excess-risk tail E and revises Theorem 2 for separate k1/k2 and learner-risk versus sample-mean-deviation terms. The original gap-based bound survives in Appendix C's Theorem 3. Appendix C generalizes U-statistic concentration to nonsymmetric kernels and independent learner randomness, with corresponding proof changes. v1's Proposition 1 and unique-optimum corollary are removed.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's broad learning applicability: v1 chiefly evaluates optimization and discrete model selection, while v3 directly tests continuous regression, six real datasets and loss-tail behavior, with uncertainty reporting for mean costs. The randomized-learner analysis and added implementation information further improve applicability and reproducibility, while reported failures clarify practical boundaries. These gains outweigh the removed standalone-DRO comparison, unique-optimum corollary and some reproducibility and limitation details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work by the same authors. All 36 pages of v1 and 41 pages of v3, including Appendices A–D, support comparison. BAG, ReBAG and ReBAG-S correspond to MoVE, ROVE and ROVEs despite the changed title and terminology.

after.justification: Section 3 and Appendix D report original stochastic-programming experiments and synthetic and real-data regression results, including mean costs, tail probabilities and confidence intervals.

before.justification: Section 3 and Appendix D report original optimization and model-selection experiments, including hyperparameter profiling, tail-heaviness tests and runtime comparisons.

C1.justification: The abstract retracts a central comparative advantage: v2 claims better trajectory stitching, whereas v4 describes stitching comparable to leading model-free methods. The conclusion also softens superior data efficiency to a high level of data efficiency, while retaining PLDM's layout-generalization advantage.

C2.justification: Sections 4.3–4.5 recognize GCIQL as competitive and revise explanations of GCRL failures, including a dynamic-programming hypothesis for short-trajectory stitching. Section 4.7 adds a hierarchical-control explanation for HIQL's Ant performance. v4 also explicitly qualifies task transfer by fixed dynamics and discusses the adapted Dreamer comparison's limitations and PLDM's inference cost.

D1.justification: Appendix J substantially expands baseline reproducibility information with grid-search procedures, dataset-specific goal-sampling and BC/AWR settings, and Ant-U-Maze baseline tables absent from v2. v4 also supplies a direct PLDM repository link and describes its environment, data-generation, training, and evaluation scripts; v2 already announced a code/data release through its project page.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same 23-dataset navigation study, including Two-Rooms data variations, Diverse PointMaze layout generalization, Ant-U-Maze stitching, and chaser avoidance. The added comparisons remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: v4 Appendix G and Table 6 add reward-free adaptations of TD-MPC2 and TD-MPC2 with inverse dynamics modeling. The six main methods, adapted DreamerV3, reconstruction baseline, and chasing-task Random/Zero comparators remain.

E3.justification: Appendix J substantially revises reported GCIQL and HIQL settings across Two-Rooms and Diverse PointMaze. For example, GCIQL's BC coefficient changes from 0.3 to 0.003 for most Two-Rooms settings, and HIQL's learning rate changes from 3e-4 to 3e-5 for short sequences. Appendix F.1 also extends replanning-frequency controls across dataset sweeps.

E4.justification: v4 extends the existing planning-time analysis with Figures 10–11, testing performance when replanning every four steps across Two-Rooms and Diverse PointMaze conditions. It also tests whether inverse dynamics modeling mitigates adapted TD-MPC2 collapse. Existing loss-component, ensemble, and HILP representation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The maze-generalization plot changes its uncertainty bands from standard deviation in v2 Figure 1 to standard error in v4 Figure 2, retaining three seeds. v4 explicitly discloses one seed for TD-MPC2+IDM. The pooled Welch tests and selected ten-seed analyses already existed in v2.

E6.justification: With revised baseline settings, Table 2 replaces GCIQL's no-door-passing success rate of 22.0 ± 1.4 with 99.6 ± 0.4. Figures 4 and 6 substantially revise GCIQL and HIQL rankings, and Tables 7–8 no longer report significant PLDM superiority over GCIQL in the Two-Rooms comparisons. New results include replanning controls and adapted TD-MPC2 success rates of 0%, or 35% with IDM.

M1.justification: PLDM retains the same architectures, JEPA prediction objective, collapse-prevention losses, predictor ensembles, and MPPI planning procedure. The model details match across v2 Appendix C and v4 Appendix D; ensemble-index notation is clarified.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v4 revises headings, explanatory paragraphs, and takeaways, uses more precise layout terminology, adds appendix navigation and acknowledgments, and relocates limitations and computational-cost discussions.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a different conference layout throughout, swaps the introductory figures, revises the overview graphic and plot markers, adds a main-text trajectory illustration and Figures 10–11, and restructures baseline hyperparameter tables. Existing appendix trajectory, ensemble, and HILP visualizations are retained and repositioned.

R1.justification: v4 adds the TD-MPC2 citation and discusses its reward-dependent representation learning relative to PLDM's setting. It also qualifies its positioning against adapted DreamerV3. The broader related-work coverage remains essentially unchanged; numerical citation formatting is a presentation change.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, training and planning objectives, collapse-prevention mathematics, and layout-distance definition remain substantively unchanged. Notational corrections do not introduce new mathematical reasoning, assumptions, or proofs.

improvement.justification: The revised baseline settings and results materially strengthen this comparative study: v4 recognizes GCIQL's strong stitching and sample efficiency and HIQL's Ant performance, correcting important overgeneralizations in v2's argument. Narrower claims, expanded reproducibility information, and additional replanning controls improve the evidence's usefulness. The added TD-MPC2 comparison remains limited by its adaptation and single-seed IDM result, but the decisive improvement is the more balanced central comparison.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PLDM study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original navigation experiments and reports revised baseline results, additional replanning evaluations, and adapted TD-MPC2 comparisons.

before.justification: v2 reports original navigation experiments, success rates, trajectory analyses, ablations, and timing measurements in Section 4 and the appendices.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes open-ended ToM and leading performance among general methods on each benchmark. V2 emphasizes scalable automated agent modeling and strongest overall performance against an expanded comparison set, including reasoning models. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion add central claims about human-like confidence estimates and online inference supporting embodied assistance.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting model confidence to human inference, uncertainty estimates to effective helping, and interpretability to correction through feedback. It removes the conclusion that automated discovery matches manually specified models. Its limitations add the lack of native multimodal inference but omit V1's specific warnings about irrelevant hypotheses, inaccurate likelihoods for similar hypotheses, and strict computational budgets.

D1.justification: V2 documents cognitive-scenario selection and captioning, household goal-generation rules, and online inference with 20 particles and a 10% filtering threshold. It adds reasoning-model identifiers, revises the belief-sampling prompt, and supplies an additional action-likelihood prompt. The original model-discovery hyperparameters and project/code destinations remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The five original question-answering benchmarks remain. V2 adds captioned cognitive-study scenarios covering online goal inference under full observability and desire/belief inference under partial observability. It also evaluates interactive household assistance on Online Watch-And-Help, extending coverage from answering questions to supporting sequential decisions.

E2.justification: V2 adds DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, and o3-mini-high, while removing TimeToM, PercepToM, and the manually specified AutoToM comparison. BIP-ALM and LIMP now have comparisons across all five benchmarks. SymbolicToM gains Hi-ToM results, although Appendix A3.4 still says it was evaluated only on ToMi. Random Goal is added for embodied assistance.

E3.justification: The original benchmark sizes, ToMi preprocessing, Hi-ToM subset, and shared multimodal text inputs remain. New protocols include six goal-inference scenarios and seven food-truck scenarios, caption adaptation, probability or seven-point confidence responses, and Pearson correlations with human judgments. Embodied assistance uses 20 episodes across four task categories, a shared helping planner, and speedup relative to an unassisted agent.

E4.justification: V2 retains the five ablation variants and both original qualitative examples. It adds substantial analysis by question type, context length, agent count, and recursion level against reasoning models in Figure 4, extending beyond V1's narrower Hi-ToM order analysis. Figure 5 adds an inference trace, and Appendix A2 adds a case showing human feedback correcting erroneous extracted information.

E5.justification: V1 reports experimental point estimates without repeated-run counts, error bars, or significance tests. V2 introduces correlation significance reporting in Table 2 and standard-error bars for embodied-assistance speedup in Figure 7, with three runs per episode. These additions concern new evaluations; they do not establish increased repetition of the original benchmark experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes AutoToM's MMToM-QA accuracy from 75.50 to 83.00 and its overall average from 80.93 to 82.43; BIP-ALM's MMToM-QA score changes from 76.70 to 56.17. MMToM-QA ablation and compute values also change. New results include human-judgment correlations of 0.93, 0.88, and 0.73, and assistance speedups of 27.7% for AutoToM versus 6.3% for Random Goal and 6.8% for GPT-4o. The PDFs do not explain the causes of all revised benchmark values.

M1.justification: The original model-discovery and Bayesian-inference loop is retained in Algorithm 1. V2 substantially extends the procedure to online goal inference: Algorithm 2 maintains, replenishes, reweights, and filters goal particles across timesteps. Appendix A2 also introduces a workflow for incorporating human feedback and recomputing an inference.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, revises terminology toward agent modeling, and rewrites substantial portions of the abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental narrative. Experiments are organized into three studies, Algorithm 1 moves to the appendix, and appendix sections are reordered around implementation, feedback, and individual experiments. The separate ethics statement is removed and limitations are integrated with the conclusion.

P2.justification: V2 switches from two columns to one and substantially reorganizes displays. V1's Figures 3 and 4 become a combined Figure 3; Figure 2 gains cognitive-study and assistance panels. New displays include condition-wise comparisons, an inference trace, feedback interaction, human-model scatterplots, and assistance speedup. Table 1 changes grouping and structure, and new correlation and goal-definition tables are added.

R1.justification: The three related-work strands and main positioning against handcrafted model-based inference remain. V2 adds citations concerning thought-tracing, DeepSeek-R1, SMC, planning with ToM, and altruistic helping, while dropping Wagner et al.'s Mind Your Theory and Ying et al.'s NIPE. These are bounded updates rather than a wholesale revision of the literature framing.

T1.justification: The original Bayesian posterior formulation, entropy-based utility, recursive-state definitions, and model-space calculation are preserved. V2 adds a limited mathematical specification of sequential weighted-particle inference in Algorithm 2, including likelihood reweighting and normalization. It introduces no new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation beyond V1's question-answering results: stronger reasoning-model comparisons, human-judgment analyses, and a controlled assistance evaluation test the psychological plausibility and practical usefulness of AutoToM's inferences. The appendices document these additions. Removing the manual-model control and several specific limitations weakens completeness, while unexplained numerical revisions and the SymbolicToM reporting inconsistency reduce transparency. Nevertheless, the new evaluations provide a substantial overall gain in support for the paper's central capabilities.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoToM, with matching core algorithms and five benchmark datasets despite changes to the title and organization. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and embodied-assistance results, plus new comparisons of model outputs with previously published human judgments. These qualify independently of the reused human data.

before.justification: V1 reports original AutoToM benchmark accuracies, ablations, computational costs, and qualitative inference results in Section 4 and Appendix A.

C1.justification: v1 leaves efficient constraint-enforcing binary sampling for future work. v2 claims a controlled log-potential sampler and an effective tau-annealed MCMC procedure. Its spherical-sampling claim is narrowed from the entire replica-symmetric region to most of that region.

C2.justification: v2 explains binary sampling failure through the persistent q=1 peak and how a diverging potential removes it. It adds qualifications concerning reference-system replica symmetry, AMP failure on correlated or structured data, and strong finite-size effects with a possible RSB-related threshold gap (Section 3 and Appendix E.2.2).

D1.justification: v2 specifies root-finding for the spherical-prior norm multiplier and explains when channel integrals are analytic. New MCMC schedules are documented. Conversely, v1's explicit outer Euler-Maruyama pseudocode is omitted in favor of a general description of SDE discretization.

E1.justification: Both versions study synthetic random spherical and binary perceptron problems. Gaussian inputs already appear in v1 Appendix A.2, alongside binary inputs elsewhere. The new potentials and algorithms retain this task coverage; structured-data applications are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 introduces direct algorithmic comparisons against standard temperature-annealed MCMC with potential U(s)=-sΘ(-s), evaluated against the proposed tau-annealing scheme in Figure 3 and Appendix E.3. v1 contains no corresponding MCMC baseline comparison.

E3.justification: New MCMC protocols use 100, 200, or N sweeps and system sizes up to 8192. Log-potential ASL experiments use T=0.5 and N=1000, 2000, 5000, and 8000, replacing cross-entropy experiments with beta=10, gamma=2 and different sizes. The retained spherical stability experiment keeps its original settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds a binary log-potential stability-distribution check against theory (Figure 2), plus analyses of MCMC sensitivity to sweep budgets and system size, including N-scaled budgets and inverse-size plots (Appendix E.3). The spherical stability validation is retained.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 5 specifies means and standard deviations over 100 runs. v2 Figure 6 reports averages over 250 simulations but does not define its displayed error bars; MCMC uncertainty details are also unspecified. These concern different experiments, so the counts do not establish increased repetitions of a retained experiment.

E6.justification: The cross-entropy success curves are removed and new log-potential results accompany a predicted ASL threshold near alpha=0.65. MCMC results support a tau-annealing threshold near 0.55 with N sweeps. These are new results under different conditions, not same-setting gains. The reported spherical frontier is also revised to fall slightly short of d1RSB.

M1.justification: v1's exploratory cross-entropy target measures are replaced by a constraint-enforcing log-potential target for binary perceptrons. v2 also introduces a distinct sampling procedure: Metropolis-Hastings with an annealed, piecewise potential U_tau(s) approaching -log(s) (Section 4.4.2).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 adds an explicit contribution list and fuller Bayesian and sampling-failure explanations, and reorganizes the appendices around a general derivation followed by model-specific applications and limiting analysis.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 1–2 are consolidated into v2 Figure 1 with a transition-detail inset. The uniform-binary plots move to appendix Figure 5, and new log-potential and MCMC displays are added. The side-by-side main-text algorithms become one full-width appendix algorithm, alongside substantial title and page-layout restyling.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly positions its formalism beyond Ghio et al.'s planted setting and its binary sampler relative to heuristic solvers. It substantially expands cited discussion of diffusion–MCMC hybrids, other ASL applications, and perceptron geometry and hardness; the cross-entropy positioning around Baldassi et al. (2020) is removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds an asymptotic analysis near q=1 explaining the obstruction for non-diverging potentials and deriving the log-potential condition T<1 (Appendix F). It generalizes replica and stability-distribution calculations to arbitrary potentials and adds reference-system and saddle-point equations, replacing the cross-entropy-specific derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves efficient constraint-enforcing binary sampling unresolved. v2 substantially addresses this gap with a theoretically motivated log potential, empirical stability checks, and an MCMC construction tested against a temperature-annealing baseline and varying budgets. It also narrows the spherical claim to match the reported transition. These gains outweigh weaker error-bar documentation and the remaining limits of finite-size and MCMC distributional validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ASL/AMP perceptron-sampling work despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, and rendered figures support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the spherical experiments and reports new log-potential sampling experiments and MCMC comparisons in Figures 2, 3, and 6–8.

before.justification: v1 reports original empirical stability distributions for spherical perceptrons in Figure 4 and cross-entropy sampling success rates over 100 runs in Figure 5.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the same enrollment strategy, two-stage training contribution, over-2.1 dB SI-SNRi advantage and 60% reduction in optimization steps. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: V3 expands interpretations of pooling trade-offs, different sensitivity to positive versus negative interferers, weak-enrollment limitations and mixed benefits from WSJ0 fine-tuning. Appendices explain clean-enrollment normalization failure, speaker confusion, omitted target speech and interfering-speech leakage. The original limitations concerning distillation, artifacts and clean-enrollment performance remain.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C supply previously unavailable data-generation and split details, VAD processing, STFT/network parameters, optimization schedules, batch size, 200k/400k training-stage budgets, and baseline adaptations/fine-tuning. V3 also explains binaural input representation and clean-enrollment preprocessing, and adds an implementation link. These are predominantly new disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to existing settings.

E1.justification: V3 adds evaluated natural recordings from Freesound and VoxConverse, MSDWild/VoxConverse speech-overlap analysis, and WSJ0 extraction tests. Its appendices also document broader enrollment-quality, duration and interferer conditions. LibriSpeech, WHAM! and the four binaural-RIR sources remain; some supplementary scenarios were already mentioned in v2 without supplied evidence.

E2.justification: Main Table 1 replaces SpeakerBeam with USEF-TFGridnet, while NMF, TCE and the binaural LookOnceToHear comparison remain. SpeakerBeam is still evaluated as TD-SpeakerBeam in Appendix J, so it is not removed from the entire paper. The new MOS comparison also includes unprocessed audio.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 add PESQ and WER to the four original metrics. The new listening study uses five recordings, ten participants and a 1–4 rating scale. Appendices supply pooling, enrollment-quality, transfer and confusion-testing protocols. The existing main evaluation retains 5000 test-clean samples; newly disclosed training settings do not establish changes to those experiments.

E4.justification: The original training/fusion ablations, interferer-duration tests and labeling-robustness study remain. V3 supplies extensive additional evidence on pooling, individual interferer types, enrollment length and quality, speaker confusion, WSJ0 fine-tuning, and successful/failing extractions. Several analyses were only cross-referenced in v2. Redisplaying the labeling study as Table 3 is not itself a new analysis.

E5.justification: Table 3 replaces labeling-study boxplots with numerical plus/minus summaries, and Tables 6–7 specify averaging inference timings over 50 repetitions. Cross-sample standard deviations and the main comparison's two-sample t-tests at 90% confidence remain. No increase in training-run or seed replication is established.

E6.justification: The original four metrics for retained methods match across v2 Table 1 and v3 Tables 1–2, including the proposed model's 8.85 dB SI-SNRi for two-speaker mixtures and enrollments. V3 adds USEF and PESQ/WER entries, extensive appendix results, and MOS scores of 3.35 for ours, 2.60 for FiLM, 1.45 for USEF and 2.10 for unprocessed audio. These are added findings, not a same-setting improvement by the revised model.

M1.justification: The Siamese TF-GridNet encoders, self-attention fusion, pooling size 40, causal extraction branch and two-stage losses remain unchanged. New pseudocode, binaural input details and clean-enrollment handling document components or applications already described or referenced in v2; they do not establish an algorithm revision.

P1.justification: The main section order, related work and conclusion remain stable. Rewriting is concentrated in the encoder-fusion explanation and convergence discussion, with additional explanatory paragraphs, an appendix outline and updated affiliation/contact/conference text. Most expansion supplies scientific documentation rather than extensively rewriting existing prose.

P2.justification: V3 redraws Figure 2, adds fusion pseudocode, splits the main results table into monaural and binaural tables with additional metric rows, and replaces the labeling boxplot with Table 3. New MOS and appendix tables, quality plots and waveform/spectrogram examples substantially expand the displays. New inconsistencies include duplicate Figure 4 labels and an SI-SDRi caption on the MOS table.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the original 37 references are retained. V3 adds references for WebRTC VAD, MOCOv3-related training motivation and target-speaker confusion analysis. USEF-TSE was already cited in v2. The broader research positioning and novelty argument remain stable.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3), the independently timed speech assumption and the formal interferer categories remain unchanged. Appendix A supplies empirical overlap statistics, and Appendix K uses cosine similarity for error analysis; neither introduces a new proof, theorem or substantively revised formal model.

improvement.justification: V3 supplies substantial implementation details and supplementary evidence that v2 merely referenced, resolving important reproducibility and evidential gaps. Real-recording evaluations, WSJ0 tests and failure analyses make practical applicability and limitations more assessable. The small MOS study and inconsistent captions and metric descriptions weaken parts of the additions, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in documented evidence and technical transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their supplied text, equations and displays are readable. However, v2 ends after its references despite citing absent appendices; v3 includes Appendices A–N. Earlier supplementary contents cannot be checked, so appendix differences below concern newly supplied documentation and evidence, not necessarily newly performed experiments.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental results and additionally supplies real-recording listener ratings, cross-dataset evaluations, robustness analyses and failure cases.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original extraction results, training and fusion ablations, interferer-duration tests, and a ten-user enrollment-labeling experiment.

C1.justification: The headline claims of first finite-sample policy evaluation and order-optimal epsilon dependence remain. The introduction now foregrounds nominal-model ergodicity in its contribution statement. Since v2 already discussed this relaxation for small radii in Remark 1 and Appendix B, this is a limited reframing rather than an entirely new contribution.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly leaves tight dependence on S, A, and the contraction factor open, explains the types of model mismatch represented by each uncertainty set, and interprets the new numerical checks as supporting contraction. The existing ergodicity and function-approximation limitations remain, with applicability further qualified by the revised radius conditions.

D1.justification: Appendix E supplies kernel formulas, numerical parameter choices, sampling budgets, and the finite-product approximation used to evaluate the seminorms. These are new implementation disclosures for the diagnostics. Code access, hardware, seeds, and complete uncertainty-sampling instructions are not supplied.

E1.justification: v3 introduces empirical coverage absent from v2: four cyclic ergodic kernels with 5–8 states, evaluated individually and under contamination, TV, and Wasserstein-1 uncertainty. These uncertainty types were already studied theoretically; their numerical evaluation in Appendix E is new.

E2.justification: Tables 1–4 introduce the span seminorm as an explicitly reported comparator for the constructed seminorms' contraction behavior. No competing policy-evaluation algorithm is empirically benchmarked.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces numerical protocols: 1,000 random directions per fixed kernel, and 30 sampled kernels with 50 directions each per robust case. The robust tests use radius 0.15 and a finite-product norm approximation with maximum length 3 and 25 products per length. v2 has no corresponding evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: New analyses test the one-step contraction underlying Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, including all three uncertainty families. They compare sampled contraction ratios with the stated contraction factors and span behavior; v2 provides proofs without these numerical checks.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports minimum, median, 90th-percentile, and maximum contraction ratios across sampled directions and kernels. These are descriptive distribution summaries; neither version supplies repeated-experiment uncertainty, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 add sixteen numerical result rows absent from v2. Fixed-kernel maximum ratios are 0.8090, 0.8718, 0.9014, and 0.8685; robust-case maxima range from 0.8134 to 0.9162, while reported maximum span ratios equal 1. These are new diagnostic findings, not improvements over earlier learning-performance measurements.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the same geometric truncation, MLMC correction, anchored value updates, and subsequent average-reward estimation phase. Added block-ending statements clarify the pseudocode without changing its procedure.

P1.justification: Related work moves from Appendix A to Section 2, the ergodicity assumption moves earlier, appendix organization changes, and a conference checklist is added. Copyediting and terminology are refined, but most existing abstract, exposition, and algorithm descriptions remain closely matched.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reformats the document into the NeurIPS style, changing the title and author block, text and equation layout, and pseudocode presentation. It also introduces four captioned numerical tables; v2 has no corresponding result displays.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of concurrent finite-sample work by Chen, Wang, and Si and two Roch-led studies, distinguishing the paper's policy-evaluation focus. It also expands citations on average-reward RL, uncertainty models, and applications, and revises the characterization of prior policy-optimization oracle access. This substantively updates positioning beyond relocating v2's related work.

T1.justification: v3 replaces all-kernel ergodicity with nominal-model ergodicity plus explicit radius conditions, substantially revising v2's existing small-radius discussion. Appendix A adds Dobrushin product bounds and joint-spectral-radius arguments; Lemma F.1 corrects v2's identification of joint spectral radius with the maximum individual spectral radius. It also revises the Lyapunov-series convergence proof and changes the stated TV Lipschitz factor from 1 to 1+1/delta in Lemma 5.3.

improvement.justification: Correcting the individual-versus-joint spectral-radius identity and adding explicit product-contraction arguments address an important weakness in v2's central proof. Revised radius conditions, Lyapunov-series reasoning, and numerical checks substantially strengthen the paper's theoretical support. The numerical checks remain approximate and the checklist incorrectly denies experiments, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the central proof improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by the same authors. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including the revised proofs and new numerical tables. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: Appendix E and Tables 1–4 report original numerical contraction tests on Markov kernels and random directions. These qualify despite the checklist's inconsistent statement that the paper contains no experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports theoretical results, proofs, and a mathematical lower-bound example, but no original experimental or simulation outcomes.

C1.justification: The central symbolic-unification contribution remains. The abstract revises its quantitative totals, and the introduction adds qualified novelty claims concerning the first LLM–symbolic-tool integration for number-theory discovery and possibly the first integration with a proprietary research-grade computer algebra system.

C2.justification: V3 explains runtime tradeoffs in the sensitivity results and why trajectory normalization removes artificial convergence acceleration from folding. It adds an interpretation of unrecovered high-degree coboundaries and an outlook involving higher-dimensional CMFs and D-finite constants. The original LLM and manual-substitution limitations are largely retained and reorganized.

D1.justification: V3 documents exact rational fitting through SymPy, 30 random recurrence checks with tolerance 10^-10, Maple minimality checking and the cluster used for sensitivity experiments. Appendix J adds filenames and detailed schemas for two supplemental pickle datasets, including formula provenance. The repository and interactive-demonstration links are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 455,050-paper corpus, subject categories, target constants and CMF trajectory/start-point ranges. V3's convergence summary and sensitivity experiments retain this coverage. Lower formula/source counts change the retained sample, without establishing a new domain or task.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 retain GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview for equivalence testing, and GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet and GPT-4o mini as extractors. The new sensitivity study varies the existing algorithm's parameters and clustering control.

E3.justification: V3 adds a substantial evaluation design: clustering-granularity and threshold sweeps with a no-clustering control, UMAPS depths from 4 to 120, and Guess depths from 8 to 500 over 100 random formulas. Appendix D normalizes runtimes to default settings, while Section 5.4 introduces trajectory-normalized convergence r/ℓ1(t). These are added protocols; the retained benchmark settings do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests whether clustering loses recoverable links, how UMAPS fitting depth affects recovery and runtime, and whether Guess recurrences generalize across fitting depths. V3 also adds false-positive examples in I.4–I.5 and CMF metric scans in G.6. V2 lacks these systematic sensitivity analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for the benchmarks. V3's random formula samples and numerical substitutions concern validation design, not repeated-run uncertainty. Its checklist adds no concrete statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 4 changes related formulas from 381/407 to 360/385 and CMF-embedded formulas from 188/407 to 166/385; source papers decrease from 154 to 140. Canonical counts, long formula-table entries and LLM scores remain unchanged. V3 adds sensitivity/runtime results and a 1,693-formula CMF summary, including 57 with reported normalized convergence 1.76. Revised totals with different denominators do not establish a same-setting performance decline.

M1.justification: The reported canonicalization pipeline adds numerical validation and Maple MinimalRecurrence after RISC fitting. The code-repair prompt also expands the supplied error excerpt from 50 to 400 characters (v2 F.6.3; v3 I.6.3). The core clustering, folding and UMAPS procedure remains; rational-function fitting was already present in v2.

P1.justification: V3 adds a glossary and NeurIPS checklist, separates Limitations from Outlook, and relocates existing coboundary proofs into a dedicated appendix. The introduction and several explanations are edited, but most existing narrative and technical exposition remain recognizable and substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 adds a substantial set of displays: four sensitivity tables (7–10) and two CMF metric visualizations (Figures 7–8). Figure 5 is enlarged to full width, and main-text floats and the formula-source table are reflowed. The long canonical-form tables retain their entries and basic design.

R1.justification: V3 expands discussion of symbolic regression and LLM–tool integration, citing PAL, ToRA, Parsel and program-search research. It adds mathematical context concerning minimal recurrences, discrete flat connections and D-finite CMFs. These additions refine the positioning while retaining the central symbolic-unification research agenda.

C1.justification: v4 elevates preservation of performance under diagonalization and generalization to other nonlinear RNNs into abstract and contribution claims. It also adds Transformers to the abstract's empirical superiority claim. The explicit v3 contribution claiming priority in scaling a bio-inspired RNN is removed, substantially changing the contribution framing.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations attributing diagonal-model performance to more efficient representations and interpreting the capacitance ablation as supporting nonlinear membrane capacitance. Appendix B.5 argues that convergence iterations impose little runtime overhead. The suggestion that adding a time feature could improve performance is removed; the existing Newton-iteration limitation remains.

D1.justification: v4 documents fixed dimensions and block counts for the additional recurrent-model comparisons, adds per-dataset timings with a 1,000-step basis, and revises the EigenWorms hidden-dimension entry. Table 6's new 'include time=False' column restates v3 Appendix B.4 rather than documenting newly changed preprocessing.

E1.justification: All six original classification datasets remain. Appendix C adds PPG-DaLiA regression evaluation, extending task coverage to continuous-target prediction within physiological time-series modeling. This is a limited benchmark expansion with a distinct prediction requirement.

E2.justification: Tables 1–3 add Transformer and RFormer comparisons, with scores attributed to the Rough Transformers paper. Table 9 introduces comparisons against MguSSM, GruSSM, and LstmSSM. The original nine baselines remain, while the evaluated comparator families expand substantially.

E3.justification: Table 6 changes the reported EigenWorms hidden dimension from 16 to 64; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects rerunning or correcting the setting. Added experiments introduce PPG-DaLiA MSE evaluation, timing over 1,000 training steps, and fixed-architecture model comparisons. The original classification splits and tuning grid remain.

E4.justification: New Tables 10–11 directly test liquid versus constant capacitance and diagonal versus dense Jacobians, addressing central architectural choices previously untested in v3. Figure 2 adds convergence-iteration analysis. The earlier state-dependence and complex-parameter ablations remain as Tables 12–13.

E5.justification: v4 explicitly reports standard errors for aggregate accuracy in Table 3 and Tables 12–13, replacing v3's unlabeled aggregate uncertainty values. The latter captions also identify per-dataset standard deviations. Figure 2 adds iteration-distribution boxplots. The retained five-seed reporting does not indicate an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v4 adds regression, runtime, recurrent-model, and architectural-control results. Table 11 reports average accuracy of 65.4 for diagonal versus 63.3 for dense Jacobians. The new Transformer row changes the EthanolConcentration ranking: 40.5 versus LrcSSM's 36.9. Original classification accuracy values remain, including LrcSSM's 66.3 average, while its Table 3 uncertainty changes from 18.6 to 8.3 under standard-error reporting.

M1.justification: The core LrcSSM equations (8)–(14), architecture, and ELK procedure are retained. Appendix D extends the existing diagonalization approach to gated RNNs, giving a GRU construction and introducing MguSSM, GruSSM, and LstmSSM adaptations. Appendix E also constructs the constant-capacitance StcSSM variant.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, NSSM/LSSM terminology is revised throughout, and Sections 3.2–3.3 provide new signposting. Appendices are reorganized, with the former Appendix C ablations becoming Appendix E. Most existing methodological, background, discussion, and conclusion prose remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v4 adds five tables covering runtime, regression, recurrent-model comparisons, and two architectural controls, plus the convergence boxplot in Figure 2. Tables 1–3 gain comparator rows, and Table 6 gains a time-feature column. Earlier ablation tables are relocated and renumbered; the architecture diagram is retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds references supporting GRU, LSTM, MGU, Rough Transformers, and PPG-DaLiA. The earlier references and main related-work discussion remain. Removing the explicit first-to-scale-bio-inspired-RNN claim modestly revises novelty positioning alongside the broader recurrent-model framing.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a gated-recurrence-to-ODE derivation, defines generalized diagonal A and b constructions, and works through the GRU case. These extend the mathematical formulation. The existing LrcSSM equations and Appendix A stability proofs and scaling arguments are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important empirical gaps in v3: Tables 10–11 directly test the capacitance and diagonalization choices, while Table 7 and Figure 2 provide concrete evidence about computational cost and convergence. These additions substantially strengthen scrutiny of the central design and efficiency arguments. Broader comparisons also expose limitations, although the retained claim of best EthanolConcentration performance now contradicts the added Transformer result, 40.5 versus 36.9. That inconsistency tempers, but does not outweigh, the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LrcSSM research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, supporting reliable comparison across relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds PPG-DaLiA results, runtime and convergence measurements, additional recurrent-model comparisons, and new architectural ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original LrcSSM classification experiments on six datasets and ablations of state dependence and complex-valued parameters, alongside results attributed to prior work.

C1.justification: Introduction contribution 2 strengthens the central multivariate guarantee by removing the explicit weight-boundedness restriction and extending the N-neuron guarantee from sparsest solutions to all ℓp minimizers for 0 < p < 1. The principal univariate claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4 replaces the discussion of required weight bounds with remaining limitations concerning functional structure, uniqueness and equivalence to ℓ1 minimization. It also withdraws the stated extensions to unregularized biases and piecewise-linear loss objectives. Experimental interpretations and the difficulty of efficiently computing p* are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 retains Algorithm 1, its balancing convention, PyTorch/Adam implementation information, experimental hyperparameters and the same code-access link. No implementation or resource-access information is added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six-point univariate peak/plateau dataset and ten synthetic points in 50 dimensions, with coordinates and labels sampled uniformly from [-1, 1]. No evaluated task or scenario is added.

E2.justification: Both experiments retain unregularized Adam and AdamW as comparators, alongside reweighted regularization with p = 0.4, 0.7 and 1. No comparison method is added or removed.

E3.justification: Appendix A.3.2 retains MSE training for 100,000 epochs, learning rate 0.01, widths 80 and 100, and regularization parameters 0.003 and 0.005 for the respective datasets. The theoretical constraint removal is not reported as a change to these experiments.

E4.justification: The comparisons across p values and the learned-function snapshots throughout training in Figure 19 are retained. No new ablation, robustness test, sensitivity analysis or case study appears.

E5.justification: Both versions document shared random initialization for the univariate comparison. Neither reports repeated-run counts, numerical seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 3 and 17–20 retain identical plotted results and learned interpolants. Both report that p = 0.4 recovers the three-neuron univariate solution and that all tested p values produce multivariate solutions satisfying the 2N sparsity bound.

M1.justification: The formal multivariate optimization in Equations (8)–(11) drops the explicit infinity-norm constraints on weight products and reformulated variables. This relaxes the proposed formulation, while the path-norm penalty, network architecture and implemented reweighted algorithm remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V3 corrects typographical errors and notation, changes appendix references from 'Section' to 'Appendix', and organizes the multivariate proofs into named steps. The overall section structure and most prose are retained.

P2.justification: All twenty figures retain their graphics, axes and legends. Limited caption edits, split equation displays and changes in figure placement relative to surrounding text alter the layout, particularly in the experimental appendix.

R1.justification: V3 credits Yang, Chen and Xiang (2022a) for the boundedness argument and adds Cover for the activation-pattern bound. It removes the corresponding Ojha, Winder and Stanley citations. The broader related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds existence proofs, extends Proposition 4.1's N-neuron bound to every 0 < p < 1, and proves p-independent boundedness, allowing Theorem 4.1 to dispense with an imposed weight bound. Lemma 4.1 now uses realizable activation patterns and explicitly bounds the number of nonzero neuron blocks. V2's Remark 2 extending the result to piecewise-linear loss objectives is removed.

improvement.justification: The new arguments in Appendix A.2 remove an important restriction on the central multivariate theorem and establish existence and an all-p neuron bound that v2 lacked. These substantially strengthen the theoretical foundation and justified applicability of the paper. Withdrawal of the bias/loss extensions narrows secondary scope, and the empirical evidence is unchanged, but the central theoretical gains support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite revisions to the multivariate theory and pagination.

after.justification: V3 retains the original synthetic-data training experiments and their sparsity curves and learned interpolants in Section 5 and Appendix A.3.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A.3 report original synthetic-data experiments, including network sparsity during training and learned interpolants in Figures 3 and 17–20.

C1.justification: The main claims remain the target-update mismatch, its remedy through a continuous imitation-trained proxy, improved stability and performance, no deployment overhead, and simple LIF neurons surpassing ANN counterparts. The abstract and introduction retain the headline improvement of up to 32%.

C2.justification: v1 explains LIF's advantage through the difficulty of approximating more complex neuron dynamics. v2 Section 5.4 instead argues that the bottleneck shifts to the RL algorithm once SNNs surpass ANNs. v2 also removes the energy discussion's 'more than two orders of magnitude' assertion and acknowledges task-dependent performance. The simulation-only limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 substantially fills the documentation absent from v1's referenced appendix. Algorithms 1–3 and Appendices A.2–A.5 specify propagation, proxy widths and learning rates, K=3 updates, neuron parameters, TD3 settings, state/action normalization and RTX 3090/Xeon hardware. The abstract also adds a code-access link. These are disclosures rather than demonstrated implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both evaluate InvertedDoublePendulum-v4, Ant-v4, HalfCheetah-v4, Hopper-v4 and Walker2d-v4. The added comparator and appendix results use these same tasks; the environment illustration introduces no additional coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds the ANN-SNN conversion method attributed to Bu et al. (2025). The existing comparators remain: Tang et al. (2021), Zhang et al. (2022) and Chen et al. (2024a) in v1 correspond to pop-SAN, MDC-SAN and ILC-SAN in v2.

E3.justification: The energy-estimation assumption changes from 12.5 pJ per FLOP in v1 to 3.97 pJ per MAC in v2; the SOP cost remains 77 fJ. The added conversion comparator uses 100 simulation steps. Newly specified settings for retained experiments are documentation additions, not evidence that those experiments were rerun differently.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.6 adds a limited sparsity comparison: average firing rates are 32% for PT-LIF and 33% for vanilla LIF. The target-output/MSE diagnostics, neuron comparisons and ANN control already exist in v1; Appendix A.6 mainly provides more detailed displays of those retained analyses.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 5(b) presents the ANN control through aggregate curves without uncertainty bands. v2 Figure 8 and Table 11 additionally report task-level variability for that existing control. Five-seed reporting, one-standard-deviation table entries and half-standard-deviation curve bands remain the general practice; no increase in runs or new significance test is established.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 returns and APGs are unchanged. v2 adds conversion results with -21.11% APG and detailed proxy-ANN results with -8.38% APG. Table 2 replaces the ANN energy estimates under different cost assumptions, reporting an average of 281.78 nJ versus 886.33 nJ in v1; however, v2's listed task values actually average 241.80 nJ. SNN energy entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Both versions replace the spiking target actor with a continuous proxy trained through squared output-matching loss and repeated gradient updates, while retaining Polyak updates for the critic. The new pseudocode and appendix disclose implementation choices, including the proxy update schedule, without establishing a redesign.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries and methodology undergo extensive rewriting and clarification. v2 distinguishes training from simulation steps, corrects terminology and cross-references, and divides the former performance-analysis narrative into Sections 5.2–5.6. It also adds structured appendices and a conference checklist.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual documentation with an environment illustration, three algorithm boxes, parameter tables and supplementary result displays. Existing learning and stability plots are retained and renumbered; Figure 1's update labels change. Table 1 gains a comparator row, Table 2 adds operation counts, and Appendix A.6 both regroups existing scores and displays detailed ANN-control results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references covering ANN-SNN conversion, direct spiking RL, off-policy algorithms and NPU energy estimation, including Bu, Cao, Sun and Millar works. It removes the noisy-SAN and Qiao references. The related-work categories and central positioning around adapting RL to SNN dynamics remain substantially the same.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 1 and its Appendix A.1 proof: under differentiability, a proxy's output change vanishes as its learning rate approaches zero. This is a limited local result, not an RL convergence guarantee. The appendix also supplies explicit SAN and neuron mathematics, while the original proxy-loss derivation remains.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially remedies v1's missing reproducibility material through explicit architectures, hyperparameters, preprocessing and training procedures in Appendices A.2–A.5. The conversion comparison and detailed ANN control also make the evidence easier to assess. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies: Table 2's ANN average disagrees with its entries, and Algorithm 3 uses current states in its Bellman target despite Equation 2 specifying next states. The improvement is principally in reproducibility and inspectability, not higher shared performance or a general convergence guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Proxy Target study and are readable throughout. v1 ends after the references despite referring to an appendix; v2 supplies Appendix A. This supports comparison of the added documentation without assuming that the underlying implementation changed.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds conversion-baseline results, firing-rate measurements and detailed results for the ANN control.

before.justification: v1 reports the authors' TD3-based MuJoCo experiments, including learning curves, five-seed return comparisons, target-output diagnostics and energy estimates.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction strengthen the central SE guarantee from O(sqrt(T) ln^2 T) to O(sqrt(T) ln T), now claiming improvement over the previous GP-UCB bound for every d ≥ 1 rather than d > 3. The main Matérn guarantee also covers a broader smoothness–dimension range.

C2.justification: New footnotes to Theorem 3 explain that the previous extra Matérn restriction resulted from omitted lenient-regret proof steps and that the extra SE logarithmic factor was avoidable. Section 4's remaining limitations and Figure 1's interpretation are unchanged.

D1.justification: The algorithm specification and disclosed simulation settings are unchanged. No implementation instructions, hardware or runtime information, or code/data access information is added or removed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same one-dimensional synthetic Bayesian-optimization scenario in Figure 1. No datasets, evaluation domains, or additional test scenarios are introduced in the appendices.

E2.justification: Figure 1 retains MVR as the comparator to GP-UCB and the idealized Case I reference curve. No evaluated comparison method is added or removed.

E3.justification: Figure 1 retains the Matérn smoothness parameter ν = 5/2, noise variance σ² = 3, 200 query steps, and the same query-frequency and information-gain measurements.

E4.justification: The illustrative analysis of query concentration and information-gain growth in Figure 1 is unchanged. Neither version adds further ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness experiments, or empirical case studies.

E5.justification: Simulation reporting is unchanged: neither version supplies seeds, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for Figure 1.

E6.justification: Figure 1's sampled function, histograms, and information-gain curves are identical. Its findings of slower information-gain growth than MVR and behavior resembling Case I from t ≥ 30 are retained; no empirical result entries change.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the GP posterior updates, and the confidence-width schedule in Equation (6) are unchanged. The revision strengthens the analysis of the same GP-UCB procedure.

P1.justification: v2 adds two correction footnotes, rewrites Appendix A.3 into separate kernel cases, and makes limited wording and notation corrections. The main narrative and section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: The new footnotes and shortened Lemma 6 alter local page layout, while the expanded Appendix A.3 reflows subsequent material. Figure 1's panels, axes, legends, and caption, and Algorithm 1's display remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The introduction broadens the claimed SE advantage over Srinivas et al. [48] from d > 3 to all d ≥ 1. The related-work section and all 59 references are unchanged, so the positioning revision is localized.

T1.justification: Lemmas 4–6 and Appendix A are substantively revised. Retaining geometric weights in Appendix A.1 improves the SE regret bound from O(sqrt(T) ln^2 T) to O(sqrt(T) ln T). Appendix A.3 derives polylogarithmic Matérn lenient regret, allowing Theorem 3 to drop 4ν² + 2νd ≥ d² while retaining 2ν + d ≤ ν². Further corrections address the constant after Equation (8), quadratic-growth constants in Appendix A.2, and the SE log-log exponent in Appendix A.3.

improvement.justification: The revised derivations resolve important weaknesses in this primarily theoretical paper: they tighten SE regret from O(sqrt(T) ln^2 T) to O(sqrt(T) ln T) and remove an unnecessary Matérn restriction. Appendices A.1–A.3 supply the supporting steps and correct additional algebraic and logarithmic terms. These changes substantially strengthen the central guarantee and its mathematical support, while preserving the empirical illustration and the qualifications concerning expected regret and optimality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GP-UCB regret-analysis work. Their complete main text, Figure 1, equations, and Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains Figure 1's original simulation results: the sampled function, 200-step query histograms, and information-gain trajectories for GP-UCB and MVR.

before.justification: Figure 1 reports an original one-dimensional Bayesian-optimization simulation, including a sampled Matérn-GP function, query histograms, and information-gain trajectories for GP-UCB and MVR over 200 steps.

Appendix F expands applicability qualifications beyond the single-neuron and low-dimensional embedding limitations already stated in v1.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a NOBLE-specific implementation link, reports approximately four days of training and the training hardware, and specifies time-grid and stimulus durations. It also documents VIP and fine-tuning hyperparameters. v1 provides architecture, optimizer, inference-hardware, and library information but lacks these substantial additions.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates NOBLE on PVALB models; v3 additionally trains and evaluates it on a VIP interneuron in Appendix D.3. VIP already appeared illustratively in v1 Figure 2, but without this NOBLE evaluation. The task remains single-neuron voltage prediction under square-pulse currents.

E2.justification: v3 adds comparison controls within NOBLE: absent, single-feature, and three-feature embeddings in Table 1, and data-only versus feature-weighted fine-tuning in Table 3. E6.justification: v3 adds extensive quantitative results, including 2.5% VIP voltage error, failure to fire without embeddings, and sag_amplitude error falling from 69.6% before fine-tuning to 9.6% with feature weighting. The headline 2.18% PVALB error and 4200× speedup persist; revised settings prevent interpreting the additions as matched-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The sinusoidal embeddings and FNO architecture remain intact. v3 adds optional feature-specific fine-tuning using a weighted combination of voltage-trace and feature losses, demonstrated for sag_amplitude in Section 4.6 and Appendix D.7.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of stochastic neuron models and distinguishes NOBLE from NeuPRINT's population calcium-imaging setting. C1.justification: The abstract narrows the critique of existing feature-description methods to automated neuron-level methods for LLMs/NLP and qualifies the single-description comparison. The three central contributions—multi-concept descriptions, quantitative evaluation, and feature analysis—and the main accuracy claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 replaces v1's proprietary-model necessity argument with open-model applicability, interprets the new ablations as robustness evidence, and develops a precision-versus-fragmentation explanation for increasing k. It adds fixed-cluster incompleteness and MAD's outlier sensitivity as limitations, and uses relative-activation diagnostics to support percentile sampling.

D1.justification: Appendix A.8 and Figure 16 add participant recruitment, compensation, completion-time information, and full study instructions. Appendix A.5 supplies identifiers and access links for the alternative generators. Existing generation prompts, benchmark implementation details, GPU and timing disclosures, and PRISM code-access information remain.

E1.justification: Human evaluation shifts from an author-only pilot to independent PhD and working-student participants from two institutions, broadening the evaluated population. The English C4, Cosmopedia, and concept-specific text coverage and feature-description tasks are retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding benchmarks retain GPT-Explain and Output-Centric with the same model-specific participation. The new evaluation-generator ablation reuses GPT-Explain; Qwen3, Phi-4, and DeepSeek R1 serve as pipeline components rather than new competing feature-description methods.

E3.justification: v3 adds protocols varying k across 1, 3, 5, and 10 and changing the LLM used separately for description generation and evaluation. Human evaluation expands from one annotator and six features to seven annotators and eight features, and adds embedding-based comparison of human descriptions. The original benchmark settings remain documented as before.

E4.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix A.5 add cluster-count sensitivity and separate generator/evaluator ablations. Appendix A.6 adds relative-activation distributions and cluster-level examples testing whether percentile sampling captures meaningful patterns. The earlier randomization and quartile analyses are retained and consolidated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Figure 6 newly reports between-participant variability through boxplots of human ratings and human-description cosine similarities, replacing the pilot's individual-rating presentation. The existing 95% AUC confidence intervals and MAD standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged; no new repeated-run or significance-testing procedure is specified.

E6.justification: The main benchmark values are unchanged between v1 Table 2 and v3 Table 1, but substantial ablation, activation-analysis, and human-study results are added. For example, v3 Table 3 reports maximum/mean AUC of 0.75/0.75 at k=1 and 0.88/0.61 at k=10, versus 0.85/0.65 at k=5. Polysemanticity results also change: Figure 5 revises GPT-2 XL feature 6067's PRISM score from 0.41 to 0.38.

M1.justification: The percentile-sampling, embedding and k-means clustering, and LLM-labeling pipeline remains unchanged, as do its core scoring procedures. Alternative cluster counts and language models are tested as ablations rather than introduced as a redesigned method.

P1.justification: v3 locally rewrites the abstract, scoring explanation, human-study summary, and limitations. It condenses the main-text sanity checks into a summary, consolidates their details in Appendix A.6, and moves some concept-space discussion to Appendix A.7. The overall section sequence and much of the existing prose remain.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reformats the document's typography, title treatment, running headers, and figure sizing. It adds four tables and three figures, revises the human-comparison display, changes plot axes and legends, reorders benchmark rows, and relocates the sanity-check table to the appendix. Existing metalabel displays are retained with revised layout.

R1.justification: v3 adds Neo et al.'s attention–MLP interaction work and the Qwen3, Phi-4, and DeepSeek R1 reports. It also qualifies its positioning toward automated neuron-level NLP interpretation. The related-work discussion and representative-method overview are otherwise substantially retained.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the formal relative-activation ratio r_j = |a_99/a_max| in Equation 9. The earlier extraction and scoring mathematics is substantively retained, with indexing, embedding notation, and control/concept labeling clarified rather than new theoretical results or proofs added.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves cluster-count sensitivity as future work, asserts model requirements without quantitative ablations, and bases human validation on one co-author. v3 addresses these important validation gaps through targeted ablations and a documented study with seven independent participants. These substantially strengthen the evidence, although robustness wording remains overstated: Table 5 shows maximum AUC changing from 0.85 with Gemini evaluation to 0.58 with Qwen3 evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PRISM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison; image-based figure content was inspected visually.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds cluster-count and language-model ablations, activation analyses, and a seven-participant human study.

before.justification: v1 reports original feature-description benchmarks, randomization checks, percentile analyses, and a human annotation pilot involving six features.

C1.justification: Sections 1.1 and 5 replace the claimed shallow-to-deep equivalence for global identifiability with a sufficient finite-identifiability result requiring restricted input counts. The claim of certifying uniqueness of given deep-network weights is withdrawn. Contributions concerning neurovariety dimensions and linear activation thresholds remain, under the revised guarantees.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 explicitly acknowledges that the techniques establish only finite identifiability for deep networks and leaves generic global identifiability as Conjecture 40. It explains that composing unique shallow networks need not preserve uniqueness. Section 3.2 also explains how the bottleneck width constrains the entire decoder, replacing the earlier emphasis on successive width increases.

D1.justification: Neither version provides an implemented training procedure, experimental hyperparameters, hardware details or code/data access instructions. Expanded proof constructions do not add implementation or reproducibility information of this kind.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or evaluated tasks. Changes to admissible network widths and degrees concern theoretical architecture conditions, not empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against a proposed algorithm. Comparisons with previous identifiability bounds are theoretical.

E3.justification: Neither PDF specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. Revised degree and width conditions are mathematical assumptions, not experimental settings.

E4.justification: Neither version contains ablations, robustness tests or empirical case studies. The new algebraic examples and counterexample support theoretical arguments assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: No empirical result entries are reported in either version. Changes to analytical bounds and symbolic examples are theoretical changes assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The feedforward PNN/hPNN models, monomial activations and homogenization construction are retained. The revisions change their theoretical guarantees rather than network architecture, training or inference procedures.

P1.justification: The exposition is extensively revised around finite versus global identifiability. Section 4 is reorganized into necessary conditions, tensor tools and the main proof. The former omnibus proof Appendix A is reorganized into topical Appendices A-C, while the neurovariety and truncation appendices move to D and E.

P2.justification: v1's Figure 1 in Appendix A.4, illustrating three two-layer network architectures, is removed without a replacement figure. The single-column format remains, with reference and appendix material reflowed.

R1.justification: The central positioning changes from claiming global uniqueness beyond prior work characterized as only locally identifiable to extending finite-identifiability theory for deep feedforward PNNs. Section 1 now acknowledges global-identifiability results for previously studied architectures. Additional references address PNN singularities, model merging and connections between finite and global identifiability.

T1.justification: Theorem 11 changes from parameter-wise uniqueness iff adjacent blocks are unique to a sufficient generic finite-identifiability theorem using minimum preceding layer widths. Appendix B replaces the tensor-lifting argument with composite-Jacobian rank lemmas and induction; Example 41 contradicts v1's uniqueness implication. Bottleneck conditions and bias-case proofs are revised. The stated universal activation bound changes from 2d_l - 2 in v1 Corollary 22 to 2d_l - 1 in v2 Corollary 17, which also allows a single output.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central correctness problem: Example 41 directly contradicts v1's Theorem 11. It replaces that assertion and its proof with a qualified finite-identifiability theorem and detailed Jacobian analysis in Appendix B. Although the guarantees are narrower and generic global identifiability becomes a conjecture, correcting the foundational claim substantially improves the paper's rigor and reliability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including the substantial replacement of the central theorem and proof.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical throughout its main text and appendices. Its new counterexample and Jacobian examples are mathematical constructions, not empirical results.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical results, proofs and illustrative algebraic examples, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes.
