C1.justification: The abstract and first contribution now explicitly claim accurate sampling and simulation of fast-folding proteins, whereas v1 left protein applications to future work. The efficiency contribution is also qualified: v1 promises no sacrifice in sampling performance, while v2 says efficiency gains can preserve high sampling quality. The central consistency and transferable-dipeptide contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges increased capacity as part of MoE's benefit, revises the earlier favorable interpretation of alanine iid performance, and develops protein fidelity-versus-consistency tradeoffs. It adds a concrete applicability boundary through umbrella-sampling failures. New kinetic interpretations are partly inconsistent: C.6.4 says MoE worsens transitions, but Chignolin Table 16 shows Both outperforming Fokker–Planck alone.

D1.justification: v2 adds learning-rate bounds, the identities of the fifteen evaluated dipeptides, detailed protein configurations, expanded hardware and runtime information, and a Langevin-update description. It also reports availability of model weights and self-contained JAX and PyTorch notebooks beyond v1's code announcement. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to every underlying implementation.

E1.justification: v2 adds Chignolin and BBA, a six-bead alanine benchmark using explicit-solvent reference trajectories, and restrained umbrella-sampling experiments. These substantially extend system size and evaluation conditions. Müller–Brown and earlier dipeptide coverage remain; moving AC and promoting KS does not constitute new coverage.

E2.justification: Table 13 introduces comparisons with Force Matching, Noise and Force Matching and Operator Forces, using published baseline results against models retrained on the corresponding six-bead system. Appendix C.2 also adds Wide and Deep capacity controls. The previous Diffusion, Two For One and Transferable BG comparators remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include protein training on 80% of reference samples, TICA-based evaluation with 100-bin histograms, the 100k-sample six-bead comparison, capacity controls and transition-state analyses. For existing alanine experiments, Both's reported regularization strength changes from 10^-4 to 10^-3 (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 3), without establishing whether this reflects rerunning or correcting the description.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ablation separating expert specialization from parameter count, protein component ablations, contact-map and nonlocal-distance analyses, and trajectory and transition-matrix diagnostics. Appendix C.7 also reports umbrella-sampling failures in poorly represented high-energy regions. These investigate substantial additional questions beyond the retained conservative-model, residual and bond analyses.

E5.justification: The existing three-training-seed alanine evaluation, ten-model toy evaluation and variation across test dipeptides are retained. Appendix B.4 introduces protein uncertainty estimates from three inference seeds using the same trained models, distinguishing inference variability from training variability. No increase in existing training repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial protein, force-matching, capacity and kinetic results. Existing results also change: alanine Both simulation PMF changes from 0.099±0.003 to 0.091±0.004 alongside the revised regularization setting; transferable Both simulation PMF changes from 0.183±0.070 to 0.203±0.104. These are revised results, not a uniform same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The conservative graph transformer, denoising objective with weak Fokker–Planck regularization, finite-difference approximation and time-partitioned experts are retained. The simplified expert-selection equation describes the same procedure, and Ours denotes the existing Both model. Added applications and experimental configurations do not establish a revised core algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method motivation are extensively rewritten around agreement between denoising distributions and learned energies. The experimental narrative now leads with alanine and proteins, while the toy study and detailed alanine discussion move into a substantially reorganized appendix. This exceeds editing associated solely with added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 creates a combined alanine/protein comparison figure and summary table, adds structural, trajectory and transition displays, and relocates existing toy and alanine figures. Main-table JS columns remain available in appendix tables rather than being deleted. Existing line plots are restyled, and the main dipeptide illustration changes from AC to KS while retaining AC elsewhere.

R1.justification: v2 extends positioning through discussions of Jamun and Target Score Matching, plus appendix connections to NETS/Hutchinson estimation, flow matching and Operator Forces. The primary distinctions from Two For One and FP-Diffusion remain. Publication updates for existing references, including Charron and Lewis, are not additional works.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds an explicit flow-matching score relation, and B.1 supplies a discrete Langevin update. The original weak-residual derivation and coarse-graining formalism remain; removing the theorem box does not remove the result. The newly written update in Equation 33 has a positive potential-gradient term inconsistent with Equation 5's force convention.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through protein-scale validation, controls for the MoE capacity confound and comparisons with force-matching methods. Structural and kinetic diagnostics, explicit umbrella-sampling failures and expanded reproducibility information substantially strengthen assessment of the central claims. These gains outweigh local reporting errors, including Equation 33's inconsistency with Equation 5 and the kinetic interpretation contradicted by Chignolin Table 16.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds protein experiments, model-capacity controls, six-bead alanine comparisons and structural and kinetic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original sampling and molecular-simulation results for Müller–Brown, alanine dipeptide and transferable dipeptide models in Section 5 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same headline claims about extending Thompson sampling to function spaces, avoiding explicit uncertainty quantification, providing theoretical guarantees and improving PDE optimization. The precise guarantee is revised within the theoretical sections.

C2.justification: V2 argues that underestimated posterior variance preserves NOTS's regret rate. V3 explicitly demonstrates the failure of that argument under repeated queries and separates the exact-posterior guarantee from the implemented approximation. It adds a heuristic small-noise justification for unmodified NOTS, substantially revising the explanation of how the theory applies in practice.

D1.justification: New Appendix D.3 specifies Gaussian observation noise with variance equal to 1% of each output coordinate's empirical variance. The H100 hardware disclosure, training hyperparameters and promised code repository are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Darcy-flow rate, pressure and potential-energy optimization, and the shallow-water inverse problem. No dataset, domain or evaluated task scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Section 6.1 and Table 1 retain RS, BO, BFO, GP-TS and STO-NTS as comparators. Appendix E retains the same comparisons involving SNOTS, NOTS and the baselines.

E3.justification: The stated grids, candidate-pool sizes, optimization budgets, model configurations and training settings are retained. V3 newly specifies experimental observation noise in Appendix D.3, but does not identify a revision to an earlier setting or a rerun; this is additional reproducibility disclosure.

E4.justification: Appendix E retains the 2048-channel single-hidden-layer FNO analysis, last-layer training setup and Figures 4–5 with the same findings. No empirical ablation, robustness test or case study is added or removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report results across 10 trials with standard-deviation shading and Table 1 standard deviations. The new checklist reiterates this practice without adding runs, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and Figures 1–5 retain their results and qualitative findings. For example, NOTS final average regret remains 0.012 ± 0.001 for Darcy flow rates and 0.134 ± 0.043 for shallow water.

M1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds a randomize-then-optimize variant that perturbs training observations with Gaussian noise while regularizing last-layer weights around initialization. This auxiliary procedure recovers exact posterior covariance; the PDFs do not establish its adoption in the reported experiments. The core NOTS algorithm remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V3 makes targeted prose revisions in Sections 3–5, reorders Appendix C, reorganizes Appendix D and adds a NeurIPS checklist. The publication footer is updated, while most of the main narrative and appendix exposition are retained.

P2.justification: The checklist introduces a new layout block, and revised text and reordered appendices alter page composition. Figures 4–5 now precede the Appendix E heading and setup text. All five figures retain their graphical content and captions, and Table 1 retains its design.

R1.justification: V3 adds Srinivas et al. on GP optimization and information gain, and Bardsley et al. on randomize-then-optimize, supporting the revised theoretical discussion. Section 2 and the broader research positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Proposition 2 changes from an O(sqrt(T)) guarantee for last-layer-trained NOTS to O(sqrt(T gamma_f,T)) for exact GP posterior sampling, with the added condition f = f_tilde composed with H. Sections 3–5 formalize the observation operator H. Appendix C supplies logarithmic information-gain reasoning, a repeated-query counterexample to the previous boundedness argument, and an exact posterior-covariance derivation for perturbed training. Proposition 1 is retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves the reliability of the central theory by exposing the repeated-query flaw behind v2's NOTS regret guarantee, narrowing Proposition 2 to exact posterior sampling, and deriving an exact-covariance training alternative. This corrects an important overstatement while preserving the empirical evidence. A material limitation remains: the assertion that the bound is approximately valid for unmodified NOTS is still heuristic.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NOTS research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete Appendices A–G are readable and support comparison, including material reordered in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains the original optimization results in Table 1 and Figures 1–5, including the Appendix E experiments.

before.justification: V2 reports original Darcy-flow and shallow-water optimization experiments in Section 6, plus single-hidden-layer FNO experiments in Appendix E.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and discussion summary retain the same central claims: efficient, geometry-based detection using pretrained representations, with strong performance across generators and encoders. The additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4 now explicitly distinguishes absolute perceptual straightening from differential straightening of natural versus synthetic videos, arguing that the latter explains detection despite negative gaps in human-vision-inspired models. New interpretations identify aggregated features as dominant and discuss shot boundaries and scene-cut frequency as potential limitations or confounds.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and identifies PySceneDetect as the tool used for scene-cut analysis. Original preprocessing, classifier settings, hardware and timing disclosures are retained. Some comparative detail is lost: Figure 2B no longer labels the selected layer for each encoder. Repository availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Section 7 adds the DeMamba one-to-many benchmark and Veo3 evaluation, extending coverage to previously untested sources such as SEINE, OpenSora, MorphStudio, HotShot, Show-1 and MoonValley. VidProM, GenVidBench, Physics-IQ and the existing natural-video coverage are retained.

E2.justification: New Table 5 compares ReStraV with NPR, STIL, TALL and DeMamba in the one-to-many experiment; the earlier detector comparison sets remain. Figure 2B also expands the evaluated encoder alternatives from eight to fourteen, adding human-vision-inspired, spatiotemporal and adversarially trained models.

E3.justification: New protocols train separately on Pika, SEINE or OpenSora and evaluate across ten unseen sources, and test the existing MLP without Veo3 training on 200 Veo3 and 200 natural videos. Added analyses specify individual-feature shuffling and scene-cut measurement on 13,000 videos per class. Existing benchmark splits, preprocessing and sampling settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds permutation importance for all 21 features, a scene-cut confound analysis, and an expanded encoder study examining whether absolute straightening predicts discrimination. These substantially extend the questions investigated. The original video-length, sampling-density and temporal-window ablations are retained in Appendix B.

E5.justification: Section 4 adds a correlation analysis between absolute straightening and detection capability, reporting rho = -0.13 and p = 0.64. Existing t-tests, ANOVA and mean-plus-standard-deviation ablation reporting remain. No explicit increase in repeated runs or newly specified seed counts is documented.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds one-to-many results: ReStraV has the highest F1 in all three training settings, while DeMamba has higher AP throughout. The Veo3 test reports 83.2% accuracy, 85.1% F1 and 86.9% AUROC. Figure 2B revises some retained encoder gaps, alongside new encoder, feature-importance and scene-cut findings. Tables 1–4 and the Physics-IQ detection scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline retains frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 embeddings, the same distance and curvature calculations, the 21-dimensional classifier input and the same classifier choices. Testing additional encoders and analyzing feature importance do not establish a change to the deployed method.

P1.justification: Section 4 is locally rewritten and reordered; related work and broader impacts are revised. Benchmark subsections become lettered paragraphs, and appendices are regrouped and relabeled A–E. Most introductory, methodological and existing experimental prose remains substantially intact, with additional caption and author-text edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 5 and figures for feature importance, Veo3 examples and scene-cut frequency. Figure 2B is redesigned as a horizontal, model-family-colored comparison; other figures are resized or restyled. Tables and appendix figures are substantially rearranged, with new running headers and takeaway-box styling. Retained plots are distinguished from newly added displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new detectors, encoder families, generators and analyses, and expands AI-safety and privacy citations. Section 2 explicitly distinguishes synthetic-content detection from trajectory-based perceptual-quality assessment. These broaden the literature context without substantially replacing the original research positioning.

T1.justification: The displacement, Euclidean distance, angular curvature and aggregated-feature definitions remain mathematically unchanged. The distinction between absolute and differential straightening is developed conceptually and empirically; no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and explanation through one-to-many comparisons with specialist detectors, an unseen Veo3 test, and analyses of encoder behavior, feature reliance and possible scene-cut confounding. These address important gaps in v1's support for generalization and its mechanistic explanation. New protocols remain briefly documented, some encoder-layer details disappear, and inherited inconsistencies such as the Plants average in Table 4 versus the prose persist. Nevertheless, the added targeted evidence and clearer distinction between absolute and differential straightening provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReStraV research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds one-to-many detection, Veo3 evaluation, expanded encoder comparisons, permutation feature importance and scene-cut measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation-geometry analyses, ReStraV detection results in Tables 1–4 and Figure 7, and sampling and temporal-window ablations in the appendices.
